claims.text: The hypothesis applies to nanoparticles containing five or more metals in equal or near-equal atomic ratios and initially forming a homogeneous single-phase solid solution.
Nanoparticles with higher initial defect density will lose their single-phase solid-solution state at lower temperatures than otherwise identical nanoparticles with fewer defects.
Nanoparticles with higher initial defect density will lose chemical uniformity at lower temperatures than nanoparticles with fewer defects.
Defect-mediated atomic diffusion accelerates phase segregation.
Controlled pre-annealing can generate samples with different defect densities while composition is held constant.
Vacancies and dislocations facilitate atomic diffusion in the target nanoparticles.
Higher defect density increases atomic mobility at elevated temperature.
Increased atomic mobility promotes faster atomic segregation.
Increased atomic mobility promotes faster oxidation reactions.
Thermal treatment can be accompanied by chemical clustering or decomposition into multiple phases in multicomponent high-entropy alloys.
Lower defect density retards diffusion-mediated segregation and oxidation.
High-defect nanoparticles will show an earlier onset of secondary-phase formation or precipitation than low-defect nanoparticles.
High-defect nanoparticles will show earlier or more pronounced oxidation than low-defect nanoparticles.
Well-annealed, low-defect nanoparticles maintain a single-phase solid solution and chemical homogeneity throughout 473–1923 K under inert conditions.
High-temperature annealing reduces defect density relative to low-temperature treatment or rapid cooling.
Oxidizing versus inert atmospheres may modulate the defect-associated stability outcome.
A lack of earlier or more pronounced phase segregation, precipitation, or oxidation in the high-defect samples relative to low-defect controls would falsify the proposed defect-control hypothesis.
